passage:
[1] The yellows of autumn require no explanation. The carotenoid pigments that produce them are present in a leaf all summer, masked by chlorophyll, and when the tree dismantles its chlorophyll in September the yellows are simply what is left. Red is different. The anthocyanin pigments responsible for scarlet maples and crimson sumacs are not unmasked in autumn; they are manufactured then, in a leaf the tree is about to discard. A dying leaf that spends energy and carbon on new pigment is a puzzle, and for most of the twentieth century botanists treated it as a side effect not worth solving.

[2] That changed when researchers began measuring what the pigment does. Anthocyanins absorb strongly in the green and blue parts of the spectrum and sit in the outer layers of the leaf, where they act as a light screen. Their production in autumn coincides with a delicate operation: before the leaf falls, the tree breaks down the proteins of its photosynthetic machinery and pulls the nitrogen back into the branch for storage. This resorption recovers a substantial share of the nitrogen the tree invested in the leaf, but it takes days, and during those days a leaf with disintegrating chloroplasts still sits in full sun. Light it can no longer use safely becomes light that damages it, generating reactive molecules that can shut the resorption down before it finishes.

[3] The photoprotection hypothesis holds that anthocyanins are a sunscreen bought for exactly this window. The evidence is largely experimental. When leaves of red-turning species are shaded during senescence, they produce less anthocyanin and resorb nitrogen about as well as unshaded leaves do, suggesting that the pigment is made in response to light stress rather than on a fixed schedule. Mutant plants unable to synthesize anthocyanin resorb less nitrogen than their normal counterparts under bright, cold autumn conditions, and the gap closes when the mutants are shaded. Red leaves are also more common on the sun-facing side of a crown and in species that grow on nitrogen-poor soils, where each atom recovered is worth more.

[4] A second hypothesis begins from a different observation: many trees do not turn red at all, and the ones that do are not randomly distributed. In the early 2000s, a group of researchers proposed that autumn red is a signal aimed not at the tree's own leaves but at insects. Aphids that lay their eggs on trees in autumn choose hosts by color, and a tree that can afford to produce a costly pigment while shutting down may be advertising that it is well defended chemically. On this account red is an honest signal, expensive enough that a weak tree cannot fake it, and aphids that avoid red trees leave fewer offspring on poorly defended hosts. The hypothesis made a testable prediction: tree species with more aphid species that specialize on them should be more likely to turn red. Across a sample of European and North American trees, they were.

[5] The two hypotheses are not rivals in every respect. A pigment could protect the leaf and deter an aphid at the same time, and a signal that happened to be useful for another reason would be cheaper to maintain. But they do make different predictions in at least one place. If red is primarily a sunscreen, it should track light and cold—it should be brighter after clear, frosty nights and duller in warm, overcast autumns, whatever the local insects are doing. If red is primarily a signal, its intensity should track the presence of aphids over evolutionary time, and species that have lost their specialist aphids should, over generations, lose the habit of turning red.

[6] Both predictions have found some support, which is part of why the question is still open. Records from long-term forest plots show that the brightest red autumns follow sunny, cold Septembers, as the sunscreen account requires. At the same time, the correlation between aphid diversity and red coloration has held up in more than one dataset, and it is difficult to explain as a by-product of light stress alone. Critics of the signaling hypothesis point out that aphids see poorly at the red end of the spectrum, so that a red leaf may look to an aphid merely dark; defenders reply that what matters is not what red looks like to an aphid but that aphids demonstrably land on red leaves less often, whatever they perceive.

[7] What has changed since the days when red was dismissed as a by-product is not that the puzzle has been solved. It is that the pigment's cost is now taken seriously, and a costly trait that recurs across unrelated lineages is presumed to be paying for itself somehow. The forest in October is, on this view, not a display but a ledger, and the question that remains is what, exactly, the tree is buying.

[1] The bell over the door of Ostrowski Clock & Watch had a crack in it, so it did not ring so much as clatter, and by the second week of June Lena had stopped hearing it at all. She came in at nine, hung her bag on the hook behind the counter, and waited for her grandfather to look up from the bench. Some mornings he did. Some mornings he only lifted two fingers from the loupe, which meant the same thing.

[2] Her mother had presented the arrangement as a favor to Lena. "You'll learn something," she had said, in the voice she used for dentist appointments. Lena had understood, without anyone saying so, that the favor ran the other way. Her grandfather had lived alone above the shop since March. The apartment had one chair at the kitchen table now; the other had been moved, for reasons no one explained, to the landing.

[3] The work itself was smaller than she expected. Most of what came through the door was batteries. A woman would slide a wristwatch across the glass, and Lena would pry off the back with a tool like a tiny crowbar, and the whole transaction took four minutes. Her grandfather did not do batteries anymore. He sat at the back bench under the lamp with the green shade, and the things he opened had names she learned slowly: mainspring, escapement, balance wheel. He worked with tweezers whose tips were finer than the lead in a pencil.

[4] It was the tweezers she noticed first. On the third Tuesday he was fitting a hairspring, a coil of blued steel no wider than an eyelash, into a pocket watch that had belonged to somebody's great-uncle. She was sweeping. She saw the tweezers approach the watch, pause a quarter inch above it, and hold there, trembling very slightly, the way the surface of a glass of water trembles when a truck goes by outside. Then he set the tweezers down, flexed his hand twice under the bench where he must have thought she couldn't see, and picked them up again.

[5] "Hand me the brass one," he said, without turning. She handed him the brass one. He did not need it; it lay untouched beside the lamp for the rest of the afternoon.

[6] After that she began to keep a kind of ledger in her head. Monday: the hairspring again, and again the pause. Wednesday: he asked her to read him the serial number off a movement, though the numbers were engraved a half inch from his nose and she had seen him read the date off a penny across the room. Thursday: a customer, an impatient man in a suit, wanted his watch regulated while he waited, and her grandfather said the machine was booked and he'd have to leave it. There was no machine. There was a small brass timing stand that had never, to her knowledge, been booked by anyone.

[7] She did not mention any of this to her mother. When her mother called on Sunday and asked how it was going, Lena said, "Fine. He's teaching me the escapement," which was true, and let the rest of the sentence stay where it was.

[8] The following week she came in early, before nine, and rearranged the bench. She did it quickly, the way you pull off a bandage. The lamp came six inches closer to the vise. The good tweezers went into the front slot of the tray, where a hand would find them first without having to choose. She took the magnifying visor from the shelf where it had been gathering dust since before her time and set it on the bench, not in the center, where it would look like a suggestion, but off to the side near the parts drawers, where it might have been left by accident. Then she went and stood behind the counter and pretended to read the battery catalog.

[9] He came down at nine. He stood in front of the bench for a while with his coat still on. She turned a page. She heard the stool scrape, and the lamp's chain, and then a long nothing that she did not dare look up into. When she finally did, the visor was on his head, pushed up on his forehead like a welder's mask, and he was bent over the great-uncle's watch, and the hairspring was going in.

[10] "The bell," he said, later, while she was closing out the register. "It's cracked. Been cracked for years." He did not look at her when he said it. "Your grandmother always said she'd get it fixed, and I always said I'd do it myself." He took a slow breath through his nose. "You could order one. If you wanted. There's a catalog somewhere."

[11] Lena said she would look. Then she reached under the counter for the catalog, which was not, in fact, somewhere; it was right there, where it had always been, and she had read it twice.

[1] The summer I turned fifteen my grandmother decided to sell the shop, and she told me the way she told me most things, by handing me a job. "Sort the drawer," she said, and set on the counter a shallow wooden tray I had never seen opened, though it had lived under the register for as long as I could remember. It was full of keys. Not the blanks that hung on the pegboard in their bright brass rows, waiting to be cut, but finished keys, each one tied with a paper tag and a name.

[2] Kessler's Lock and Key had been on Fremont Street since before my mother was born. My grandmother had run it alone since my grandfather died, and she ran it the way she did everything—with a pencil behind her ear and a conviction that most problems were mechanical if you looked at them long enough. She could tell a house key from a padlock key across the room. She could tell, from the way a man held his broken key, whether it had snapped in the lock or in his pocket. Since I was nine I had spent every summer on the second stool, learning to feed a blank into the duplicator and watch the tracer ride the original's ridges while the wheel cut the copy.

[3] The keys in the drawer, she explained, were duplicates that had never been collected. Someone would come in, order a spare, pay a deposit, and not return. "You give them a week," she said. "Then a month. After that it's not theirs anymore, but it's not yours either." So she tagged them and put them in the drawer. There were more than two hundred.

[4] I sorted them by year at first, because the tags were dated in her small square hand, and the oldest went back to 1971. Then I started reading the names. Some I knew: the Albrights, who had lived two doors down from us until their divorce; Mr. Pham from the bakery, who had died the winter before. But most were strangers, and I found I could not stop building them. A woman named Dolores Ortiz had ordered a mailbox key in 1984 and never come back for it, and I decided she had moved away suddenly and forgotten the deposit. A man named Wendell Crane had left a car key in 1993, and I decided the car had been stolen before he could collect it, which was sad, and then I decided he had simply bought a new car, which was not.

[5] "You're making up stories," my grandmother said, without looking up from the lock she was rekeying.

[6] "They're keys to something," I said. "Somebody's door. Somebody's car."

[7] "They were," she said. "Locks get changed. Cars get sold." She set down her pick. "Half of those keys don't open anything anymore. That's why nobody came back for them. People know when a thing is finished before they know they know it."

[8] I did not believe her, or did not want to, and I said so. She shrugged and went back to the cylinder in her hand. But that evening, after she had turned the sign, she came and stood beside me at the counter and picked one key out of the tray without looking at the tag. It was a brass house key, worn smooth at the shoulder, and its tag read Kessler, 1988.

[9] "That one's ours," she said. "The old house on Linden. Your grandfather had a spare made the year we sold it and then couldn't stand to give it back to the new people. He kept it in his coat. I found it after he died and I didn't know what to do with it, so I put it in the drawer with the others."

[10] "Does it still open the door?"

[11] "I've never tried." She turned it over in her palm. "I don't think I want to know. If it does, I'd want to go in. If it doesn't, that's a whole other thing." She put it back in the tray, not in its place by year but on top, where I would see it. "Keep sorting," she said. "And don't throw any of them out. I don't care what the new owner does with them. That's his drawer now."

[12] I finished the drawer in three days. I sorted the keys by year, and then I did something I did not tell her: I made a list in the back of a school notebook, every name and every date, two hundred and eleven of them, and Kessler, 1988, at the top. I still have it. I have never been back to Linden Street, and I have never looked up Dolores Ortiz, though it would take me a minute now. I think I understand, finally, what my grandmother meant that evening, though I would put it differently. It is not that the keys don't open anything. It is that they open something only so long as no one tries them.

[1] For roughly a century, from the 1870s to the 1950s, the American house had a face, and the face had a mouth. The front porch—a roofed platform raised a few steps above the yard, deep enough for chairs, open to the street—was so nearly universal in that period that its absence on a new house required explanation. Pattern books sold to builders assumed it. Mail-order house kits shipped its columns in numbered crates. In the towns of the Midwest and South especially, a street was less a row of houses than a row of porches, each one occupied, on a summer evening, by people who could see and be seen.

[2] The porch did not begin as a social instrument. Its ancestors were practical: the verandas of colonial outposts in hot climates, where a roofed perimeter kept sun off the walls and let air move through open doors; the stoops of Dutch townhouses, where a raised entry kept floodwater out. What the nineteenth century did was to take these functional appendages and enlarge them until they became rooms without walls, and then to furnish them—with swings, rockers, and wicker—until they became rooms one was expected to sit in.

[3] Sitting in them had rules, though no one wrote the rules down. A person on a porch was at home and yet available. A neighbor walking past could call a greeting and expect one back; could stop at the foot of the steps and talk for a while; could, if invited, come up and take a chair. Each of these stages carried a different degree of intimacy, and the architecture made the gradations legible. The steps were a threshold; the railing was a boundary that permitted conversation across it; the front door, behind the porch, was a second and more serious threshold that most passersby would never cross. The porch was where the private household and the public street negotiated their terms.

[4] The historian Ruth Ambler, whose work on domestic architecture has shaped most recent discussion of the subject, puts the point in a way that has been quoted so often it has become almost a proverb: "The porch was never a room. It was a sentence the house spoke to the street, and when we stopped building porches we did not fall silent so much as change the subject." Her argument is that the porch's decline should be read not as a loss of sociability but as a redirection of it—toward the backyard, the automobile, and eventually the screen.

[5] The decline itself was swift. Three changes, arriving together in the decades after the Second World War, made the porch first unnecessary and then undesirable. Air conditioning removed the reason to sit outside on a hot evening. The automobile transformed the street from a place people walked through into a place they drove through, and a porch facing a stream of cars offered neither quiet nor company. And television gave the household a new focal point, one located in the interior and demanding darkness. Builders of postwar subdivisions, working to tight budgets and fast schedules, dropped the porch almost overnight and replaced it with a token stoop or nothing at all. The back patio, walled by fence and shrubbery, took over its furniture and abandoned its audience.

[6] Ambler's reading has not gone unchallenged. Some scholars object that "changing the subject" understates what was lost: a backyard patio may host the same barbecue, but it does not permit the unplanned, low-stakes contact with neighbors that the porch made routine, and it is precisely that kind of contact, they argue, that builds the trust a neighborhood runs on. Others note that the porch's golden age was also an age of intense social surveillance, in which being visible from the street meant being judged from it, and that the privacy of the patio was for many households a relief rather than a loss.

[7] The porch's partial return since the 1990s complicates the story further. Planned communities built on so-called traditional principles now require porches of a specified depth, and the porches are duly built. But visitors to these developments often report that the porches sit empty. Critics of the revival suggest that this is because a porch is not a cause of neighborliness but a symptom of it: the nineteenth-century porch was occupied because the street was already full of people worth greeting, and building the platform does not summon the parade. Defenders reply that habits take longer than a decade to form, and that the children now growing up in front of these porches may use them as their grandparents did.

[8] What both sides accept is Ambler's underlying insight, that a house is an argument about how its occupants wish to meet the world. The porch made one argument. The garage door, which now occupies the position on the facade that the porch once held, makes another. Whether the newer argument is worse is a question about which reasonable people differ; that it is different, no one seriously disputes.

[1] The bell above the door had been replaced. Corinne noticed that before she noticed anything else—before the smell of machine oil and lemon polish, before the wall of clocks ticking out of step with one another, before the man at the bench in the back who did not look up. The old bell had been brass and had rung flat, like a spoon dropped in a sink. This one was bright and even, and it seemed to her an unreasonable thing to have changed.

[2] "We close at five," Walter said, still bent over whatever was in front of him. He had a loupe screwed into one eye and a pair of tweezers in his right hand, and the hand was steady. She had half expected it not to be.

[3] "It's ten past four," she said.

[4] The tweezers stopped. He did not turn around, but she watched his shoulders do something complicated—rise, hold, settle—as if he were lifting a weight he had set down years ago and had hoped never to pick up again. Then he took the loupe out of his eye and laid it on the felt, and turned on the stool, and looked at her.

[5] "So it is," he said.

[6] She had rehearsed several openings on the drive up the coast, and all of them abandoned her now. What she said instead was, "You changed the bell."

[7] "The other one cracked." He said it as though it had happened last week, though she could see from the tarnish on the mounting screws that it had been longer than that. "Kept ringing anyway. Sounded worse every year. Finally I thought, a person ought not to have to listen to that."

[8] "I liked it."

[9] "You would." There was no unkindness in it. He stood, slowly, one hand flat on the bench, and she saw that he was shorter than she remembered, or that she was taller, or that memory had simply been generous. "You'll want coffee. Kettle's where it was."

[10] It was. So was the tin of grounds, and so, on the shelf above the sink, was the blue mug with the chip out of its handle—the one she had dropped on the flagstones the summer she was nine and had cried over as if it were a living thing. She had assumed he'd thrown it out. She took it down and filled it and did not say anything about it, and neither did he, though when she came back into the front room with it he glanced at the mug and then away, and she understood that he had seen her see it.

[11] "Business good?" she asked.

[12] "Nobody fixes anything anymore. They buy new." He shrugged. "But the ones who do come, they come a long way. I had a fellow from Halifax in March with a carriage clock his grandmother brought over. Two months I had that thing apart." He nodded toward the wall, where a dozen pendulums swung at their own private tempos. "Most of those are waiting on parts I have to make myself."

[13] She drank the coffee, which was terrible in exactly the way she remembered. Outside, a gull landed on the sill and regarded them both through the glass with one yellow eye. Walter went back to the bench, but he did not put the loupe back in. He picked up a small brass wheel and turned it over in his fingers, examining nothing.

[14] "I saw the notice," she said finally. "In the paper. About the building."

[15] "Ah." He set the wheel down. "That's why."

[16] "That's not why."

[17] He let it go, which she had not expected. In the old days he would have pressed the point until one of them left the room, and it had usually been her, and the door had usually made the bell ring its flat cracked note behind her. "They want to put up condominiums," he said. "Glass and steel, right out to the seawall. Your mother would have written letters. I don't write letters."

[18] "I could."

[19] He looked at her a long moment. On the wall the clocks reached the quarter hour in a ragged volley of chimes, none of them agreeing, and he waited for them to finish before he answered, as he had always waited, as though the clocks had a right to speak first.

[20] "You still have the key?" he said.

[21] She did. It was on the ring in her pocket, between the key to an apartment three hundred miles away and the key to a car she no longer owned. She had never once used it since the day she left, and she had never once taken it off.

[22] "Good," Walter said, and put the loupe back in his eye. "Then you can lock up. I'll be a while with this."

[1] In 1890, an American farm family that wanted its mail had to go and get it. Letters and newspapers waited at the nearest post office, which might be a corner of a general store five or ten miles away, and a farmer who could spare the trip only on Saturday read Tuesday's news on Sunday. City residents, by contrast, had enjoyed free home delivery since 1863. The gap was not an oversight; it was a matter of arithmetic. A letter carrier walking a dense city route could serve hundreds of households in a day, while one riding a country road might pass a dozen.

[2] Rural Free Delivery, or RFD, began as an experiment. In 1896 the Post Office Department established a handful of trial routes in West Virginia, largely at the urging of farm organizations that had spent a decade petitioning Congress. Many members of Congress and most postal officials expected it to fail on cost. It did not, at least not by the measure that mattered politically: farmers who received a route wanted to keep it, and farmers who did not receive one wanted to know why. By 1902 the service was made permanent, and within a decade more than forty thousand carriers were covering routes that together stretched around the globe many times over.

[3] Historians who study RFD are less interested in the mail itself than in what the mail dragged along behind it. The first and most visible consequence was roads. The Post Office would not establish a route where a carrier's wagon could not pass year-round, and it would suspend one where a bridge had washed out or a stretch of road had turned to mud. Farmers who had resisted road taxes for decades discovered that a graded, drained road was the price of a mailbox at the gate. County records from the period show a pattern repeated across the Midwest and South: a petition for a route, a rejection citing road conditions, a burst of local spending on gravel and culverts, and a second, successful petition. The federal government had found a way to build rural roads without paying for them.

[4] The second consequence was commercial, and it produced the service's most durable enemies. A farmer who no longer had to travel to the post office no longer had a weekly reason to visit the general store attached to it. At the same time, the daily arrival of newspapers and mail-order catalogs put the prices and stock of distant retailers in front of households that had previously known only the local merchant's. Small-town storekeepers organized against RFD and, after 1913, against parcel post, which allowed the same carriers to bring packages up to the gate. Their objections were not foolish. Rural storekeepers had extended credit through bad seasons and had served, along with the post office they often housed, as the town's information exchange. The catalog did none of that. But the storekeepers were arguing against a service their own customers had petitioned for, and they lost.

[5] The third consequence is harder to measure and, for that reason, the one historians argue about most. Daily mail changed what a farm family knew and when it knew it. A daily newspaper arriving by carrier was a different object from a weekly one collected on Saturday; it could carry commodity prices that were still current, weather that had not yet arrived, and political news a family could act on before the question was settled. Some scholars have argued that RFD helped nationalize rural opinion, exposing farm households to the same news cycle as city ones. Others caution that the evidence for this is mostly anecdotal, drawn from the letters of the articulate few, and that circulation figures show rural families choosing regional and agricultural papers over metropolitan dailies well into the 1920s.

[6] What is not in dispute is the change in the physical landscape. The roadside mailbox, standardized by the Post Office in 1915 after years of improvised lard cans and cigar boxes, became the marker of an address where there had been only a name. Route numbers gave farmsteads a location that a stranger could find. The carrier, who came every day but Sunday, became for many families the most regular visitor they had, and route records show carriers delivering medicine, relaying messages, and, in at least a few documented cases, driving the sick to town.

[7] It is tempting to describe all this as the countryside being pulled into the modern world by a government program. The record suggests something less tidy. Farm families asked for RFD, paid for the roads it required, and then used the connection it provided in ways the Post Office had not planned and the storekeepers had feared. The mail was the least of it.

On Saturday mornings the market hall at Ostrel smells of rind and wet stone, and for ninety years its business turned on one object: a brass beam scale at the far end of the room, facing the glass case by the hall door where the market keeps its old iron weights. A farmer would carry a wheel of cheese to the scale, the weigher would call the weight aloud, and buyer and seller would strike their bargain on that number. The buyers were village families, shopkeepers from up the valley and, lately, restaurant buyers who drive up from the city of Tessaly before dawn.

For thirty-eight years the weigher was Anselm Dray. Ask the council why the public weighing mattered and you will hear that the weighing fee, a few coins a wheel, paid for the upkeep of the hall from 1934 on. Mira Coll, a Tessaly sociologist who has studied the market for two years, calls the weighing the one habit that drew the whole valley into one room, and buyers like to say they trusted a weight they heard called aloud. Dray's answer was about the brass itself. Accounts were settled at the hall door once the weighing was done, and he liked to say that in thirty-eight years no buyer had come back to complain. “The stall scales drift with the weather,” he told me. “This one is truer than any of them.”

Dray announced his retirement two winters ago, and the council had to decide what came next. His niece, Tamsin Dray, had stood at his elbow on Saturdays since she was fourteen and had learned the scale from her uncle, down to the half-turn he gave the pan before every wheel. Odile Sarr, who chairs the council, came to its first meeting carrying the letter in which the restaurant buyers asked for a fixed price, and a sheet of her own sums showing what each cheese would fetch if the market were to price each wheel as a whole. Jory Ambel, a young goat-cheese maker, spoke for letting vendors weigh at their own stalls, and a supplier's brochure for a digital scale to replace the brass one went round the table with a quote for what it would cost to buy one.

That spring the council borrowed a digital scale for a month and set it beside the brass one. Its speed pleased almost everyone. The queue, which on busy mornings grew too long and reached the hall door, shrank to a handful of people, and the vendors who had complained of lost sales when buyers gave up and went home stopped complaining. That month an inspector from the provincial weights office tested both machines. The brass beam, he found, was out of true; worn at its pivot, it had been reading light, putting every wheel a little under its real weight.

Coll had been reading the market's sales ledgers, which go back to 1934, and after the inspector's visit she reread them. The hall's weights could be set against the weights the dairies record when a wheel leaves the press, and for at least eleven years the hall's figures had run a steady fraction under the dairies'. “It was small enough to vanish in any single sale,” Coll said. “Over a decade it was the whole margin of a small farm.” Sarr had figures of her own that summer, showing that the city restaurants had become the market's largest buyers, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to buy a digital scale of its own. Tamsin, who had offered to keep the brass scale, was asked instead to run the new one, and the habits her uncle had trained into her carried over. Sarr's sums went back into her folder. What decided the vote, she said, was the inspector's report: a beam worn out of true would have to be recast, and recasting it would cost more than a new scale. The fee still pays for the upkeep of the roof, Tamsin still weighs any disputed wheel twice, and most vendors still check their cheese on their own stall scales.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The queue was short even on a busy morning. Tamsin set each wheel on the digital pan and read the figure from the screen; she still calls it aloud, out of habit, though everyone can see it. The brass scale has been moved into the glass case by the hall door, its beam wired level. The restaurant buyers, who weigh every wheel again in their kitchens, tell me the numbers now match to the gram. Waiting my turn, I caught myself looking past the screen to the case, the way you glance at a chair someone used to sit in. The lesson Ostrel took is a sound one, that a market should have its scale tested before it trusts it. I only wish the test had come out the other way.

Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending Piet Osker wrote after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. I used to tell choirs that Osker had faced blank paper, that the Agnus Dei was his from first bar to last, a copyist's act of nerve. When the cathedral asked me to prepare a new edition, I went to the library meaning to cut his ending and print only what Corran left.

That ending has had a long life. At the premiere Osker played the organ himself, a slight figure the newspapers did not name, and the chapter liked what it heard well enough to sing the Mass every Easter afterward. Generations of singers learned its closing pages, the tower bells ringing over the last chord, as Corran's own work. A story in the choir held that she had finished the movement and that her pages were lost, and the story made each year's performance feel like a faithful copy of something real.

In the library I found a folder of Corran's pencil sketches, eleven pages, with Osker's fair copy beside them. I went through them bar by bar. Almost every phrase I had credited to Osker sits in her pencil: the melody, the bass, even the bell part, added in her margin and circled. Her pencil runs out eight bars before his close, and those eight bars carry on the line she was tracing, in the direction she was tracing it. Tucked into the folder was Hanne Corran's letter of 1949, recalling her sister's wish that the Mass end as it began. Some colleagues have wanted to build a close from that sentence. It came twenty-one years late, and by then the pages had said more than any memory could.

A few singers asked whether we should simply stop at the last bar Corran wrote, where her pencil stops, and once, in rehearsal, I stopped the choir there. The sopranos sang Osker's last chord anyway, out of habit, and then looked at me as though I had dropped something. The new edition keeps every one of his bars, set in the same type as hers, because the join between them is a matter of handwriting more than of music. On the night the tower bells rang over the final chord as they have every Easter since 1930, and I conducted those closing pages as Corran's Mass, which, I had learned, is very nearly what they are.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker is usually remembered as the copyist who presumed. The record suggests a modest man with a deadline, which is a less romantic story than the legend and a more useful one. In January 1929, weeks after Corran's funeral, the cathedral chapter announced that her Mass would be sung at Easter of the following year, and Osker's first dated page of the completion is from the same month. Hanne Corran's request that he finish her sister's work arrived that autumn, when he was already copying the last movement fair. The firm of Varlow, the Breckholm publisher, took an interest only after the premiere had filled the cathedral, and the story that Osker had once heard Anneliese play the ending at her piano first appears in a memoir of 1952.

His fair copy is the best witness to how he worked. Every bar he supplied himself carries a mark in the margin, a small pencilled cross, and there are only thirty-one of them; the rest is Corran's line, copied out by a man who knew whose music he was handling. Where her pencil grows faint, he follows the faint line instead of improving on it, and where she left two chords stacked as alternatives, he copied both into the margin and chose the plainer. His letters from that year say almost nothing about the Mass, and the reviews of 1930, which praised the ending as pure Corran, show only that the seams were well hidden. The crosses show that he left them visible for anyone who cared to look.

The chapter, for its part, voted that summer to sing the Mass every Easter with Osker's ending, and it has kept that promise for most of a century. Varlow's account books show the firm buying the publishing right from Hanne, not from the chapter, in 1934; the sketches stayed in the library with the fair copy; and the tower bells that ring after the final chord were a bell-ringer's habit long before anyone wrote them down. Each Easter, Breckholm sings an ending that is more Corran's than the legend of the presumptuous copyist allows, and it owes that to thirty-one small crosses and to the man who was honest enough to make them.
